prize_parts.citation: for empirical analyses of how import competition and technological change reshape labour demand, local labour markets and wage inequality

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: B022 with Autor, Hanson and Dorn, and B014 and B012 as alternatives. The exchange did not move me because nothing in it changed the grounds of my choice. The strongest grounds are that the work asks a first-order question, uses explicit designs and widely available data, and has had roughly a decade of replication, re-analysis and open dispute. I weight that scrutiny record heavily as a metascience-minded member. A finding that has been challenged by many independent teams and kept its qualitative core is a firmer basis for a prize than one whose causal reading is still being established. The five-of-eleven count in the chair's summary is not part of my case. I answer the chair's question on wording as follows. The citation should rest on the empirical evidence only, with no 'conceptual' claim and no claim over the task-model theory whose originators (Acemoglu, Levy, Murnane) are outside the credited set. I propose: 'for empirical analyses of how import competition and technological change reshape labour demand, local labour markets and wage inequality.' I would also want the Scientific Background to treat the shift-share critiques and the re-analyses of persistence directly. The attribution is the cleanest available: Autor, Dorn and Hanson jointly authored the China-shock papers, and Autor and Dorn also co-authored the polarisation work, so one citation names both the trade and the technology channels.
statement.case_against: The reservations are real and I do not minimise them. Shift-share identification is sensitive to critique, and the size and persistence of the China-shock effects have been qualified in re-analyses, as far as I can judge from colleagues' accounts and my general knowledge. The 2024 prize touches adjacent themes, so a B022 citation must be narrow and honest about what it names. The prize would reward a research design and measurement programme more than a conceptual advance, and some members will weigh that against it. A three-name limit also leaves out Katz, whose claim on the earlier skill-premium literature is genuine but belongs to a different citation. Finally, I cannot say B022 beats B012 on common criteria of originality, confirmation and attributable credit. B012 is very mature and has clean two-name credit. My preference rests on a judgement about explanatory reach and the scrutiny record, not on a decisive scientific gap.

responses.point: Boppart prefers B012 (Melitz and Helpman). He argues that firm heterogeneity has been confirmed on firm-level microdata for twenty years and spread into productivity, macro and policy evaluation, and he treats B022's attribution and the contested persistence of the China-shock effects as unresolved.
responses.response: I accept that B012 is the more mature framework and that its attribution is tight at two names. I do not read the open debate on B022 as a weakness relative to B012. The debate concerns magnitude and duration, and the finding that adjustment is slow and costly has, to my reading of the openings, survived re-analysis. By contrast, as Boppart and Strömberg both say, B012's welfare conclusions depend on functional-form choices such as the Pareto productivity distribution. I would not call either set of results decisive. The question is where I give weight. I give it to a body of work whose designs and data are open and which independent teams have stress-tested, and that is why B012 stays an alternative and not my lead. If the Committee chooses to recognise trade, I would not oppose B012.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B012 first. He values a model built to explain firm-level facts and then confirmed on new data, and he treats B022's persistence and magnitude estimates as still being revised. He says B022 may be the better choice if the Committee weights societal significance more than conceptual foundation.
responses.response: That is a fair statement of the trade-off, and I would add one qualification. Confirmation on new data is a criterion I share, and B022's evidence has been tested in the same way, on many datasets, by critics as well as supporters. The difference between us is which kind of scrutiny I weigh more, and I will not pretend that is settled by evidence. I agree that the two ballots cover different ground. B012 explains how trade reallocates activity across firms, while B022 documents who bears the adjustment costs of trade and technology. If the Committee must compare them on originality, breadth of confirmation and attributable credit, I find B012 slightly ahead on breadth and B022 slightly ahead on the scrutiny record. I would not defend that ordering as scientifically decisive.

responses.point: Fredriksson prefers B029 (Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn). He argues that structural demand estimation and dynamic industry models are mature and cleanly attributed, and he takes the credibility debate between structural and reduced-form approaches seriously. He names B022 as his first alternative.
responses.response: I agree that the BLP attribution is clean and that the tools are in daily use. My own reservation is about what I can check from the supplied evidence. Structural estimates depend on functional-form, instrument and equilibrium assumptions, and the replication record for those estimates is harder for me to read than for the design-based work in B022. I read that as a limit on my judgement, not as a flaw in the case. I also note that you name B022 as a fallback, which suggests that the two ballots may not be far apart on your common criteria. If you can say what evidence from merger retrospectives or out-of-sample predictions shows the estimates hold up, I would take it seriously. On methods versus discovery, I would put the weight on whether the citation names findings about market power and welfare.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson now prefers B022, as I do. Her citation adds 'conceptual' to 'empirical' analyses, and she keeps B014 as an alternative on sequencing, not substance.
responses.response: I agree on B014 and on sequencing. I would drop 'conceptual' from the citation, though. The credited set can support a claim about the empirical evidence on trade and technology shocks, but the task-model theory has originators outside it. A 'conceptual' claim would invite the very attribution objection that Hassler, Krusell and Teorell raise. If the Committee wants to name the task framework, it must widen the names or accept an overstated citation. I prefer the narrower wording, which is the most defensible reading of what these three authors produced.

responses.point: Teorell now proposes Autor, Hanson and Dorn. He ties the citation to the empirical evidence on labour demand and adjustment, and he treats the persistence debate as a question of size and duration, not whether adjustment costs exist. He is uneasy about the 2024 prize overlap.
responses.response: I agree with the trio and with the framing. On the 2024 overlap, I would call it a timing judgement and not a judgement on merit. The 2024 prize concerned the effect of institutions on long-run prosperity, while B022 concerns how trade and technology shocks redistribute within economies. I would rather the Committee state openly that it treats these as distinct discoveries than leave the proximity unspoken. I share your view that a carefully worded citation answers the credit problem better than switching candidates.

uncertainties: How far the shift-share critiques and the re-analyses of persistence should qualify the award, and whether the Scientific Background can state them without weakening the finding that adjustment costs are real.
Whether the Committee reads the 2024 prize as a reason to delay B022, and whether that is a timing view or a view about merit.
Whether B022 or B012 comes ahead on common criteria. I find the two close and cannot settle it from the evidence supplied.
Whether B014 will be judged mature enough in a future round, given that its neighbourhood-effect evidence is still being tested and credit is spread over a large team.
My attribution and replication judgements rest on general knowledge and the colleagues' round-1 files. I have not independently verified them.
statement.conflict_note: No change since round 1. From the supplied profile, none of my frequent co-authors or networks (Camerer, Brodeur and the Institute for Replication, Johannesson, Rand, Nowak, Pfeiffer, Holzmeister, Huber, Nosek) appears among the credited names on B022, B014 or B012. My SSE tie to Johannesson, a former committee member, and my work in replication and metascience shape the weight I give to scrutiny records. I treat that as a disposition, not as a tie to any candidate. Stockholm affiliation matters only for B047, which I do not propose. Katz appears on B014 and Helpman on B012, both alternatives. I have no link to either, and I disclose them without adjudicating.
